newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE-Debt conversion to lock EMU into place.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Debt conversion to lock EMU into place.

text.p: Fixing European exchange rates may be the most visible move in creating a single currency, but the conversion of debt into euro paper is meant to set it in stone.

Plans to convert quickly a large part of the stock of outstanding European debt into euros is gathering momentum, going beyond a 1995 agreement that participating governments' bonds will be issued in the single currency from 1999.
"I think we should find a way so that the important part of (German) public debt can be translated into euros," Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing told a conference last month.
France has led a drive to get government debt issued in euros, which it sees as one way of ensuring there will be no turning back on European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"It's a sign of confidence. It's a signal of irreversibility," said Stefan Collignon, director of research at the Association for the Monetary Union of Europe.
After conversion, the practical and technical problems in unravelling a Europe-wide euro-denominated bond market mean that only a very serious crisis could prompt a reversal of the move.

For France, settling the debt question was important enough that it regarded this as a reasonable trade-off for dropping its opposition to naming the new currency the euro at a summit of EU leaders in Madrid last December.

At that time it wrested a compromise whereby all new issues from 1999 must be in euros, while individual countries can choose to convert their existing stock of debt any time up to 2002 -- when national coins and banknotes go out of circulation.
France said it would convert its entire debt stock in 1999.

German banks are lobbying hard to get German debt converted quickly, overcoming, among other things, resistance to issuing debt in foreign currencies which dates back to Germany's postwar determination to prevent a repeat of 1930s hyperinflation.
Bundesbank Deputy President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said in September that it was in Germany's interest to convert existing government debt into euros from 1999.

Such a move would prevent a split in the market which would lead to a loss of liquidity and competitiveness, he said. Government bonds in national currencies which make up the euro can trade alongside those in euros in the early stages of EMU.

Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told Reuters earlier this month he believed Belgium should convert its stock of debt into euros as soon as possible. But he said it would have to look into the technical and legal issues involved.
Most other countries have yet to announce their plans.
BEHIND THE POLITICS ARE PRACTICAL HEADACHES
Technicians in national capitals getting ready for EMU are keen to make sure their own markets are as liquid as possible as this can attract business and keep the cost of funding low.
France's banking and government officials are trying to get a head start by working out exactly how debt should be converted, hoping to make French debt the euro benchmark.
They believe French debt should be among the easier to convert. It is fully dematerialised (no longer in the form of bearer bond certificates), standardised and easily negotiable.
But how will France convert franc bonds, traded in round numbers, to euros? A franc-euro exchange rate, expected to run to five decimal places, would create paper in unmanageable numbers.

The French Treasury is looking at various methods, including fragmenting government bonds (OATs) which currently have a minimum denomination of 2,000 francs, into 2,000 holdings with a denomination of one franc, official sources say.
Once converted, the issues could be rebundled into round numbers in euros although there might be initial difficulties as operators tried to match up their bits and pieces of debt.
"It might create a bit of indigestion at the beginning," Credit Lyonnais bond analyst Iain Lindsay said.
Governments may have to repay some of the odds and ends, though French official sources say this is likely to represent a small amount of outstanding debt.
Retail investors could retain their bond holdings at awkward numbers, while big market players who want round numbers will be dealing in such large quantities that bundling will be easier.
SCRAPPING MINIMUM DENOMINATIONS
Europe's governments may also use the switch to euros as an excuse to scrap minimum denominations altogether, allowing trading in theory down to the last euro.
"One could decide to use the change to have tranches of one euro. It would improve the flexibility of trading on the market, particularly for derivatives products," one French Treasury source said.
Already medium-term French notes (BTANs) have no minimum denomination, although markets trade in big amounts.
That too would probably be the case for euros.
Otherwise operators would charge a higher price to buy or sell in smaller sizes. "Economic discipline forces an unwritten denomination on the market," Lindsay said.

The absence of a minimum denomination would boost liquidity in the strip market, where coupon repayments are stripped from the bond itself and traded separately. At the moment stripped coupons carry a denomination derived from the original bond. Without this restraint, they would be more interchangeable.
France, with the leading strip market outside the United States, is keen to make sure it keeps this position after EMU, and has a clear incentive to scrap denominations, analysts say.
Britain is also looking at the possibility of scrapping denominations, bond analysts say.
USING THE ECU MARKET TO PREPARE FOR EURO
Another option being considered is to step up issues in Ecus ahead of EMU to smooth the transition to the euro. Ecus will be converted one-for-one for euros on January 1, 1999.
"One of the paths worth exploring is to use the Ecu market in the preceding months," one French Treasury source said.

A report by bankers and the Bank of France earlier this year -- meant to provide a basis for debate rather than official proposals -- recommended that the Treasury issue "a sufficient volume of Treasury bills and negotiable debt" in Ecus from 1998 onward with a maturity after January 1, 1999.
France and Britain are the only countries to have regular Ecu issuance, while France is also considering adding Ecu Treasury bill issues to its existing programme.
French banks and back-offices are likely to be ready by the middle of next year to deal with Ecu-bill issues.
But the Ecu market is still starved of liquidity and has shown little sign of a real pick-up ahead of the launch of EMU.
As a result, countries which borrow in Ecus run the risk that when they repay in euros, they will be making these repayments in a stronger currency.
"We have to be pragmatic. We are not going to go against our own interests," one French source said.
